newsitem.title: UK: Bosnians urged to set up central bank.
newsitem.headline: Bosnians urged to set up central bank.

text.p: The international community urged Bosnia on Wednesday to take charge of its own economic development and pressed it to set up a central bank to ensure the effective channelling of reconstruction aid.
Addressing a high-level conference on Bosnia's progress towards peace, British Prime Minister John Major said the West was not prepared to help the Bosnian economy forever.
"In 1996 the international community took the lead in kick starting the economy of Bosnia and Herzegovina...but there is a limit to what the international community can do," said Major.

"We look to you to take the lead to set up the central bank, to pass the necessary legislation and to recognise that in today's open trading environment economic cooperation is not an option but a necessity," he told Bosnian leaders.
More than 50 delegations attended the start of the two-day Peace Implementation Conference, called to assess the war-ravaged country's first year of peace and to set goals for the second.

Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said it was urgent that effective institutions should be established to govern Bosnia's two mistrustful entities -- the Moslem-Croat Federation and the Serb Republic.
"The council of ministers and key agencies, such as a central bank, must be up and runnning in 1997 if assistance is to be channelled effectively," he said.
"Economic recovery should be taking hold...(and) the Bosnian people must see their stake in peace."
International bankers close to the reconstruction process say a central bank is vital for distributing aid and negotiating the former Yugoslav republic's outstanding debt.

Bosnia's ambassador to the United Nations, Mohamed Sacirbey, said the country already had a framework for a central bank, with a governor and three deputies chosen to represent the state's three ethnic communities.
"It is set up -- it is just a question of its functioning," he said, adding this should be possible during the coming year.
Sacirbey urged the international community to stick to the terms of the Dayton agreement that ended 43 months of war as a precondition for distributing money for reconstruction.
"Conditionality is a factor and our president wants to see it applied," he said, but added it was in Bosnia's interests to see the whole state on a sound economic footing.

Bosnia's Serb Republic, frozen out in the reconstruction stakes for flouting key aspects of the Dayton accord, is lagging behind the Moslem-Croat federation which has received 98 percent of the $1 billion rebuilding aid disbursed so far this year.
The West says it is not underestimating how hard it will be to create a unified economy while wartime scars remain.

The problems are underlined by differences over the design of banknotes and in inflation -- the Serb Republic is notching up between 35 and 65 percent while the Moslem-Croat federation has virtually nil.
At present the German mark is used for most transactions.
The international community's high representative for Bosnia, Carl Bildt, rejected attempts to lay the blame for patchy progress at the door of the West.
"We will simply not accept that authorities which have failed in their duties to their own people should seek to put the blame for their own shortcomings on the international community," he said.
